A five-room flat in Bedok was just sold for $1.54 million, setting a new record high for HDB flats in the town
article:
A five-room flat at 152B Bedok South Road , part of Bedok South Horizon , was sold for $1.54 million ($1,266 psf) in October 2026. This is the highest resale price recorded for an HDB flat in Bedok. It is also the first HDB flat in the town to sell for more than $1.5 million.

Located on the 13th to 15th storeys, the 1,216 sq ft flat has a remaining lease of about 94 years. The transaction surpasses the previous Bedok record of $1.48 million ($1,217 psf), set by another five-room flat in the same block and storey range (see Table 1).

All 10 of the highest HDB resale prices in Bedok were for five-room flats at Bedok South Horizon. The development consists of eight blocks of 16 to 18 storeys with 940 flats in total. These comprise 457 four-room flats, 274 five-room flats and 209 two-room flats.

The project reached its five-year minimum occupation period (MOP) earlier this year. Its first resale transactions were registered in April 2026.

Since then, 60 of its flats have been resold. Of these, 36 recorded resale prices of $1 million or more. All 12 five-room flats resold so far fetched at least $1.265 million.

Within the top 10, the six flats on the 10th storey and above sold for between $1.40 million and $1.54 million. The four flats below the 10th storey sold for between $1.30 million and $1.38 million. As all 10 flats are the same size and have similar remaining leases, this suggests buyers are paying a premium for higher floors.

The subject flat’s high price could be attributed to its long remaining lease and its proximity to the upcoming Bedok South MRT Station, which is expected to open by the end of 2026 (see Map 1).

Bedok South MRT Station is on the Thomson-East Coast Line, which offers direct access to the city centre. Sungei Bedok, the next station on the line, will be an interchange with the Downtown Line.

Temasek Primary School is within 1km radius of the subject flat. Nearby, a mixed-use GLS site on Bayshore Drive, next to Bedok South MRT Station, was sold for $2.13 billion ($1,323 psf ppr) in July, EdgeProp Singapore reported. The site is slated for about 1,280 homes, a retail mall and a bus interchange.

title: More shophouses sold in 3Q2026 while leasing activity sees uptick
article:
Buyer interest in Singapore’s shophouse market continued to strengthen in 3Q2026, logging an increase in the number of caveated transactions, according to Huttons Asia’s latest quarterly report on the shophouse market.

A total of 21 caveats were lodged for shophouse transactions in the latest quarter, up from the 16 caveated deals in 2Q2026.

“The segment continues to attract wealth, underpinned by favorable interest rates, constrained supply, and foreign ownership regulations elsewhere in the property market,” said Lee Sze Teck, senior director of data analytics at Huttons Asia.

Transaction volume and quantum of shophouses in 1Q-3Q2026

Meanwhile, the total transacted quantum stood at $157.7 million in 3Q2026, 18.6% lower than the previous quarter’s $193.7 million.

Despite the decline in transaction value, Huttons’ report noted that the drop reflects “a normalised baseline” after the previous quarter was boosted by the $70 million sale of three adjoining shophouses on Lorong Liput.

That said, higher-value deals continued to dominate shophouse transactions in 3Q2026, with more than 70% of the properties sold during the quarter fetching more than $5 million.

For the first nine months of 2026, caveats show that 51 shophouses were sold, down 25% y-o-y from the 68 caveated deals during the same period last year.

The total transaction value also declined, falling to $441.3 million in the first nine months of 2026. That is 31.5% lower than the $644.5 million recorded in the year-ago period.

During the latest quarter, 999-year leasehold and freehold shophouses accounted for 81% of total transaction volume, with deals concentrated in Districts 8 and 15, Huttons said.

Lee added: “Investors generally preferred 999-year leasehold or freehold shophouses for wealth preservation.”

Among the largest shophouse deals in 3Q2026 was the sale of a unit along South Bridge Road , which topped the list at $16.8 million.

This was followed by a shophouse along Circular Road , which was purchased for $16.2 million by investor Roman Scott, chairman of The Calamander Group.

Top 5 shophouse transactions by quantum in 3Q2026

Leasing momentum picks up

In the shophouse leasing market, the number of rental contracts rose by 4.2% to 800 in the third quarter, from 768 in the second quarter this year.

This came on the back of restaurant openings, including Árō Singapore, Assaggi, Casa Lola and KIN-NOMI, Huttons noted.

Median rents during the latest quarter remained unchanged on a q-o-q basis at $6.47 psf per month.

Median rents and rental volume of shophouses

In District 2, median rents grew the most for the second consecutive quarter, increasing 8.9% q-o-q to around $7.35 psf per month.

Looking ahead, Huttons expects Singapore’s shophouse market to remain resilient through the rest of the year, supported by the city-state’s status as a “premier destination” for ultra-high-net-worth individuals to preserve and manage their wealth.

Shophouses are also among the few real estate asset classes with minimal foreign ownership restrictions, which has resulted in tightly held ownership.

“Coupled with limited supply, shophouse valuations remain well-supported over the long term,” said Lee.

title: What's moving the market: Singapore's biggest property deals and hottest searches (Oct 9)
article:
Here is this week’s data-led look at Singapore’s property market, covering record transactions, rental benchmarks and the most searched homes on EdgeProp.

The following insights are compiled from EdgeProp Buddy , URA Realis and data.gov.sg, downloaded as of Oct 6.

Non-landed private homes — new launches, resales and rents

The most expensive condo unit sold during the past fortnight was at Sky@Eleven on Thomson Lane, fetching $9.38 million. The 42nd-storey apartment changed hands on Sept 23.

Next on the list was a 10th-storey unit at Grange Residences , transacted at $9.25 million; followed by a 26th-storey apartment at UpperHouse At Orchard Boulevard , which went for about $7.77 million.

Among new-launch condos, the projects with the most transactions in the 14 days to Oct 6 included Amberwood At Holland , Union Square Residences , and The Sen .

The 212-unit Amberwood At Holland launched for sale on Sept 24 , moving 11% of its units during the weekend at an average price of about $3,019 psf.

In the Outside Central Region (OCR) or suburbs, the most popular rented condos were Lakeville on Jurong Lake Link, Coco Palms on Pasir Ris Grove, and J Gateway in Jurong East. They saw 42, 41 and 40 deals respectively.

In the OCR, three of the condo units with the highest rents — for leases starting in August — were located at Grand Duchess At St Patrick’s. They are bringing in monthly rents of $14,000, $11,500 and $10,500. The freehold condo is next to St Patrick’s School and a roughly seven-minute walk to Marine Terrace MRT Station.

Parc Botannia, The Woodleigh Residences and Eco made the list of the most transacted resale condos over the past fortnight.

Landed homes — highest transacted prices and rents

A freehold corner terrace house on Sunset Way commanded the highest transacted price in the landed property market during the fortnight ending Oct 6, when it was resold for $9 million on Sept 22. That works out to $1,764 psf on its land area of about 5,101 sq ft.

Next, a semi-detached house sitting on 3,002 sq ft of freehold land on Aida Street fetched about $8.64 million in a new sale. The home is located in the Opera Estate landed housing enclave in Siglap.

In the rental market for landed homes, the 10 highest monthly rents within the OCR ranged from $17,300 for a house on Conway Circle, to $24,000 for a detached house on Chestnut Avenue.

HDB flats — top prices and rents, most transacted blocks

In the HDB resale market, a five-room flat in Bishan was sold for $1.71 million. Located at Block 273A Bishan Street 24, on the 37th to 39th storeys, the unit is part of the Natura Loft DBSS project.

Meanwhile, the HDB flat with the highest rent was an executive unit at Block 155 Bedok South Avenue 3. It is bringing in $5,500 per month on a rental contract that began in October.

title: Frasers Hospitality enters leadership transition as CEO Eu Chin Fen steps down
article:
Frasers Property has announced that Eu Chin Fen will step down as CEO of its business unit, Frasers Hospitality, effective Jan 1, 2027.

The move follows the successful privatisation of Frasers Hospitality Trust in 2025 and the completion of the trust’s portfolio optimisation as at Sept 30, according to an Oct 9 release.

Eu joined the firm in 2011, taking on a central role in guiding the strategic growth of Frasers Hospitality. She worked closely with group leadership on the $2.1 billion portfolio optimisation of Frasers Hospitality Trust, which paved the way for the redevelopment potential of the Fraser Suites Singapore site into a mixed-use riverfront development. The site will feature a new  flagship 184-unit Fraser Suites serviced residence.

Since taking the helm at Frasers Hospitality in 2023, Eu has helped maintain the group’s industry standing.

Panote Sirivadhanabhakdi, group CEO of Frasers Property, said: “On behalf of the board, I would like to express my sincere appreciation to Chin Fen for her dedicated leadership and valuable contributions over the past 15 years.”

Chew Han Song will continue to lead as COO of Frasers Hospitality, reporting to the group CEO. He will drive global brand stewardship for this sector, expand the portfolio through third-party management agreements, and deliver operational excellence across properties worldwide, Frasers Property said.

Meanwhile, current chief financial officer of Frasers Hospitality Eric Gan will lead asset management under group investment, reporting to group COO Tony Lombardo.

Eu said: “It has been a privilege to lead Frasers Hospitality and work alongside such a dedicated, world-class team.”    “By drawing on our deep extended-stay capabilities and staying true to our commitment of warm, intuitive hospitality, we elevated guest experiences across our properties with a genuine culture of care,” she added.

title: The Toh Crescent resort home and garden an agronomist spent nearly two decades nurturing, now asking $12 mil
article:
CS and Michelle Liew have lived in Toh Estate , in the Changi and Loyang area of District 17, since 1994. “We know the area well,” says Michelle.

For CS, who spent up to 70% of his working life travelling, proximity to Changi Airport was a significant advantage.

When the family grew to include three young sons, the Liews decided they needed a bigger home. But they wanted to stay within Toh Estate. “I love the serenity of the East Coast, especially Toh Estate,” says CS, a Singaporean. “Toh Crescent is very serene and very green.”

While househunting in the early 2000s, they came across a plot along Toh Crescent, a street with predominantly detached houses. An old, single-storey bungalow sat on the freehold site of about 9,652 sq ft. CS was intrigued by the weed-covered house and, more importantly, the terrain of the land. He had even envisioned what the new house would look like once the old one was torn down.

“It was a beautiful piece of land,” he says. “There was a slope coming down, and I said to Michelle, ‘We should keep it as it is; we shouldn’t flatten it.’”

They called the property agent whose number was on the “For Sale” sign at the gate. When they could not reach him, Michelle contacted another agent, who in turn got in touch with the owners.

Back in 2005, the asking price was $2.3 million. Recognising that the owners were from Hong Kong, CS offered $2.28 million, as the figure sounded auspicious in Cantonese. The wife called her husband in Hong Kong, and they sealed the deal on the spot.

They appointed architect KC Kan & Associates to design their new home. “We had seen a property he had designed which had the kind of tropical feel that we liked,” says Michelle.

A home with the garden and pool as a focal point

From the start, the couple made it clear they did not just want to build a house. “We wanted a home that made the most of the garden and natural lighting, with the pool being the focal point,” she adds.

She wanted the home to be a private retreat for the family. The couple personally selected the materials, finishes and fittings. “We wanted something timeless,” she says — a choice that has served them well.

Completed 1.5 to two years later, the new home is a two-storey detached house with a basement that fits three to four cars, and a built-up area of about 5,136 sq ft. Keeping the original sloping terrain paid off: the basement sits at street level, while the pool deck is raised on the first level, overlooking the garden.

The upper level of the L-shaped house has five en suite bedrooms and a family room. The master bedroom has a private balcony that adjoins a jacuzzi pool deck, a walk-in wardrobe and a resort-style bathroom. Each son had his own en suite bedroom. A corner room with an en suite balcony and garden views became CS’ home office.

On the first level are a living room, a bar, an indoor dining room and an open kitchen. However, most of the time, the family prefers to dine at the alfresco dining area next to the pool deck, which overlooks the pool and the garden. It is also where people tend to congregate when they entertain at home.

“The house lends itself to entertaining,” says Michelle. “It’s easy to move between the outdoor and indoor spaces, making it perfect for having drinks at the bar and dining on the pool deck.”

The first level also has a home cinema, a guest suite with an outdoor deck, and a room that serves as Michelle’s office. A helper’s room with an en suite bathroom sits at the back of the house.

As the house was well-built, they have not had to make any changes in close to two decades, notes CS.

Favourite spots

Michelle’s favourite part of the home is the balcony overlooking the garden and the surrounding greenery, where she keeps an exercise bike and a yoga mat. “It’s such a treat to exercise surrounded by greenery,” she says. “I also love the way the house looks towards the pool and the garden.”

CS’ favourite spot is the pair of lounge seats on the pool deck, facing the pool and the garden below. He loves sitting there after work to enjoy the sunset, watching the sunlight streaming through the tree canopy.

“I used to always sit there to read magazines, newspapers, or just gaze at the pool,” he says. When it rains, he especially likes watching the raindrops falling into the pool.

‘A passionate gardener’

The garden is CS’ creation. “He is a passionate gardener, and it has been his pride and joy since we moved in,” says Michelle. “He has continued to develop it over the years.”

It has some unusual plants and regularly attracts hornbills. An old chiku tree, already on the land when they bought it, has been carefully preserved.

Armed with a double degree in agronomy and pest management, CS knows that a flourishing garden depends on understanding plant nutrition and which fertilisers to apply. “You often run into nutritional problems, micronutrient deficiencies,” he says. Knowing the symptoms and remedies is essential.

Understanding pests and diseases, and which fungicides and insecticides to apply, is equally important. “That knowledge becomes very useful in the maintenance of a garden,” he says.

His expertise was built over a career in crop protection that took him around the world, and the garden bears its marks.

After graduating from Iowa State University, CS joined Ciba-Geigy in Malaysia. A year later, US-based crop protection company Uniroyal Chemical recruited him in Singapore to oversee its entire Asia Pacific market — from China, Japan, Taiwan, South Korea to India, Pakistan and Sri Lanka, and on to Australia and New Zealand. He was only 23.

After 11 years with Uniroyal, he spent seven years with Nufarm before starting his own firm, Pacific Agriscience, in 1998. “In the early years of Pacific Agriscience, we were basically trading in generic pesticides that we sourced from India and China, and we sold those all over the world,” he says.

Travel souvenirs

Wherever his work took him, if he came across an interesting plant or flower, he would buy a pot or take a cutting home to plant in his garden.

Fruit trees and edible plants in the garden include papayas and sugarcane from Thailand, along with edible bananas, pineapples and purple chillies from across Southeast Asia.

His favourite transplant is the “100 hands banana”, grown from two seedlings he brought back from Chatuchak Market in Bangkok 18 years ago. One bunch grew to 2.5m long. “That was an all-time record,” he says.

The trees became a talking point for the foreign dignitaries, ambassadors and business associates he frequently entertained at home. These associates would give CS samples of new plant nutritional products, fertilisers and pesticides, which he would trial in the garden. “I like to experiment with them,” he says.

CS finds gardening “very therapeutic” and “a real joy” — from trimming old leaves and branches to watching new plants and flowers grow.

Just as his garden has evolved over the decades, so has his business. Drawing on the network he has built over his career, CS has reinvented himself over the past 15 years. From trading in pesticides in the early years, the business has moved into mergers and acquisitions, helping start-ups raise capital and find global partners.

Now semi-retired, CS still travels frequently. Over his 46 years of work, he has paused his travelling only twice: six months during SARS in 2003, and about 18 months during the Covid-19 pandemic in 2020.

New chapter

With three sons now grown up — two working in London, and the eldest married and living in Singapore — CS and Michelle find the house too large for just the two of them. That prompted their decision to sell the property.

“We feel it’s the right time,” says Michelle. “It’s been a wonderful family home, but our lives have changed, and we’re ready for a new chapter.”

They have appointed Gavan Lee, principal head of district at PropNex Eminence Landed, as the exclusive marketing agent. Lee is indicating a guide price of about $12 million for the home. Based on the site area of 9,652 sq ft, the land rate works out to $1,243 psf.

As the property is well-maintained, Lee expects the new owner would need to undertake only minor renovations. “The property appeals to those who want a resort lifestyle,” he says.

Now that the house will be sold, Michelle says what she will miss most is “the feeling of being away from everything”. That feeling was strongest during the pandemic, when the family gained a renewed appreciation for their home. “When so much of the world was restricted, I realised how fortunate we were to have created a home where we could swim, exercise, enjoy the garden, dine outdoors — it really was a sanctuary.”

The garden is “definitely” something CS will miss, and he hopes it will go to the right owner. “Being an agronomist and agriculturist, of course I love plants, and I love my garden. I hope the garden will stay.”

His biggest fear is that the new owner will tear up the garden, or pave or tile over it. “In fact, I told Michelle if the new owner needs me to look after the garden, I’ll be very happy to do so because I know all the plants in the garden,” he says. “I planted them, each and every one of them.”

title: How St Regis Residences owners reinvigorated their ageing luxury asset for the long term
article:
More than a decade after St Regis Residences Singapore was completed in 2008, parts of the luxury condo were beginning to show their age. By 2020, council members of the Management Corporation Strata Title (MCST) decided it was time to act.

An asset enhancement initiative (AEI) was proposed for the 173-unit development on Tanglin Road.

Among the most active council members was retired ambassador Jaya Mohideen — Singapore’s first female career ambassador. She was also one of the early buyers when St Regis Residences was launched off-plan in June 2006. She had purchased a unit for her daughter and sits on the council as her proxy.

Developed jointly by City Developments Ltd (CDL), Hong Leong Holdings and TID — a joint venture between Hong Leong Group and Mitsui Fudosan — St Regis Residences was billed at launch as the first St Regis residential development in Asia. It is linked to the adjoining 299-room St Regis Hotel Singapore.

Several council members surveyed residents in April 2020 on what they wanted improved. Beyond the wish list, however, were more fundamental concerns. The sinking fund was considered underfunded, while units at St Regis Residences were trading at a discount to some of the other luxury condos in prime District 10.

“We thought that perhaps we were not investing enough in the property, and it was getting a bit dated,” says council member CM Rajoo, who was subsequently appointed chairman of the AEI committee.

At the time, the sinking fund stood at just $1 million, according to Rajoo. The MCST subsequently raised about $6 million over a year, raising it to $7 million.

The multi-year AEI — which included the overhaul of the common areas, repurposing underused facilities, and aligning the development with St Regis brand standards — eventually cost about $10 million, excluding consultancy fees, says Rajoo. Including fees, the total was about $12 million.

More significantly, it showed how far the owners were prepared to invest collectively to keep their homes relevant and, ultimately, protect their value. “We decided to focus on things we could do to elevate the project,” Rajoo says.

Bringing Marriott on board

Marriott International, which added St Regis to its portfolio after acquiring Starwood Hotels & Resorts in 2016, was involved with the entire AEI exercise to ensure that brand standards were fully met.

Marriott has a renovation programme for its branded residences worldwide. Under the programme, soft furnishings are typically refreshed every seven years, while hard finishes are refreshed every 14 years. St Regis Residences Singapore had not undergone a major refurbishment since completion and was due for a makeover.

In November 2020, Marriott International’s global residential operations team visited the site and recommended improvements, including maintenance standards and repairs to common areas. It also proposed introducing preventive maintenance and engaging Marriott Global Design to develop the scope of works.

With Marriott Global Design involved, the AEI committee selected British interior design and architecture studio 1508 London from a list of approved firms. Its luxury residential portfolio includes No. 1 Grosvenor Square, The OWO Residences by Raffles and Regent’s Crescent in London.

The committee also engaged RSP Architects Planners & Engineers, the original project architect for St Regis Singapore, to ensure the proposed works complied with local building requirements. COEN Design International was appointed the landscape architect, and Light Collab the lighting consultant.

Everyone involved in the AEI, including the architects and designers, underwent a detailed presentation on the St Regis brand DNA. The aim was to ensure the refreshed development reflected the brand not just in its design, but also in details such as scent, toiletries, and music in the lobby and gym.

Hands-on involvement

When Rajoo presented the proposed AEI programme at a town-hall meeting in October 2021, it received 95% support from owners. The next 12 months were spent on detailed design and planning before the project went to tender.

Sunray Woodcraft Construction, part of Sunray Group, was appointed the main contractor in 2022. One of Singapore’s largest fit-out firms, Sunray has worked on projects including the restoration of Raffles Hotel Singapore, and the interior fit-out of Marina Bay Sands and Shangri-La Singapore.

For the council, that experience mattered because the works had to be carried out within an occupied luxury residence.

The project proved more complicated than initially envisaged. Construction began in February 2023 and was originally scheduled for completion in March 2024. The official handover was delayed until August 2024, with defect rectification continuing into 2025.

The committee became heavily involved on site. Rajoo says he walked the grounds daily and found himself debating seemingly minute details with contractors, down to the dimensions of the architraves.

Their hands-on involvement reflected how closely the owner-occupiers were engaged with an AEI whose outcome they and their neighbours would have to live with every day.

Rethinking the arrival experience

One area of improvement was the sense of arrival. Previously, the guard post sat in the middle of the entrance, creating a single entry and exit point for residents and visitors and sometimes causing bottlenecks.

Relocating the guardhouse further inside allowed for two car lanes: one for visitors stopping at the guard post and another for residents to proceed directly to the car park. The work was complicated because the fire command centre and cabling had to be moved, Rajoo says, but it solved a longstanding functional issue.

The team also tackled other shortcomings at the same time. A new canopy provides better shelter between the residential towers, while seating was added to the arrival lobbies. The concierge centre was upgraded, and the network of narrow ground-floor passageways — which Rajoo describes as “a maze of corridors” — was widened and given clearer identities through improved lighting and finishes.

The development has three main lift lobbies and 10 private lift lobbies on the first level. Each private lift lobby was given a distinct identity through its artwork and mantelpiece.

Not every design idea survived. The team at 1508 London had proposed a large monolithic sculpture resembling a rippled metal sheet at the entrance. The committee chose instead to introduce Traveller’s Palm plants, similar to those at Raffles Hotel Singapore.

“We wanted more vegetation to make it warmer and more welcoming,” says MCST chairman Aditya Vikram Lodha.

The choice illustrates the owners’ unusually hands-on role: they were not simply approving a design package, but also questioning how individual elements would feel for residents returning home every day.

For the committee, an important principle was that the enhancements should integrate seamlessly with the original development. The objective, says Rajoo, was to make the old indistinguishable from the new.

Making old spaces relevant again

The AEI also involved rethinking how people used the facilities. “Ultimately, it’s about making the spaces relevant,” Lodha says. “What was relevant 20 years ago may not be relevant today. There is no point having facilities that no one uses.”

Of the development’s 11 key amenities, eight were either upgraded or replaced.

At the top of residents’ wish list was to have a larger gym. That means extending the gym over part of the pond. To do that, the pond had to be drained, and support structures built below. The koi were temporarily housed at a koi fish hotel for 12 months during the works.

The result is a state-of-the-art gym that is now double its original size and features the latest gym equipment.

While the koi pond was being rebuilt, the old filtration system was also replaced with a new one. The yoga deck next to the koi pond was extended to conceal the new filtration system.

Meanwhile, an underused landscaped area next to the yoga deck was converted into a lawn, which is now used as an exercise and children’s play area.

The former private lounge was upgraded and renamed The Drawing Room. It is now used for informal gatherings and meetings. The little-used cigar room became The Library and was expanded to create a brighter, more flexible room.

The idea to incorporate workspaces into The Library emerged during the Covid pandemic, when residents wanted somewhere outside their apartments to work. Mohideen visited WeWork and other co-working spaces for ideas, but instead of placing a large communal table in the middle, she suggested orienting the workstations outwards to take advantage of the views of the greenery and the pool.

The Library is now popular with residents working remotely as well as students doing their homework, Mohideen notes.

“Since the walls were changed to glass, there is more light, the room is more cheerful, and the space is well used by the residents,” Lodha adds.

The playground was rebuilt to meet current safety codes. A pedestrian path was created for residents who want to go to the hotel. They no longer have to cut through the children’s playground to do so. The pool area was also upgraded, with topiary added to provide more privacy from the adjoining hotel restaurant.

The AEI was also a chance to address defects and shortcomings in the original development. “This wasn’t just a renovation,” says Rajoo. “We decided to make good on all the issues that had been identified over the past 10 to 12 years, and fix them systematically.”

Putting St Regis brand back into St Regis Residences

While some changes were primarily functional, others were intended to strengthen the link between the residences and the St Regis brand.

The interiors of St Regis Singapore draw on the brand’s “Metropolitan Manor” design language, rooted in the character of the original St Regis in New York. Meanwhile, its more contemporary exterior reflects the brand’s “Glass House” aesthetic.

Rather than reproducing the hotel’s Metropolitan Manor aesthetic, 1508 London reinterpreted it in a contemporary-classic style for the residences.

The palette includes natural stone, white marble, limestone and travertine, with bronze detailing and formal architectural elements such as mantelpieces and architraves.

Marriott also encourages individual St Regis properties to have elements that reflect its local identity. At the residences, the committee adopted botanical motifs inspired by Singapore flora.

The local connection extended to artworks in the lobbies and common areas by renowned Singapore artists that the MCST acquired.

Among the more distinctive additions are the handcrafted Herbarium crystal chandeliers featuring Singapore-inspired pressed flowers and foliage, by Czech glassmaker and design brand Lasvit.

The lobby entrances also feature Lasvit-designed crystal screens bearing the St Regis plaque.  The scent and music associated with the St Regis Singapore hotel were also introduced into the lobbies of the residences.

“These are soft touches that really transform the place from being ordinary to extraordinary,” MCST chairman Lodha says.

Not everything old was discarded. Some of the original Poltrona Frau furniture in The Drawing Room and The Library was retained and reupholstered after the committee recognised its quality. New pieces from the same Italian brand were added where necessary.

The guiding principle, Rajoo says, was not to replace everything for the sake of appearing new, but to preserve what was worth keeping and spend where quality mattered.

Next phase

The scope of the project also grew to address ageing infrastructure and defects where possible. More recently, the MCST spent close to $750,000 on the pneumatic waste system, and the council is already planning for the next capital-expenditure cycle.

“We recognise that the building is ageing, and that we need to change the lifts in the next couple of years,” says Lodha. “We don’t want to wait until a lift collapses and then say, ‘Oh, we should do something.’”

Knight Frank manages the estate on behalf of the MCST. Han May Leng, the residential general manager at St Regis Residences, joined in 2023 just as the AEI works were getting underway.

Having witnessed the transformation firsthand, Han says the AEI combined design improvements with practical changes to create spaces residents can enjoy in their daily lives.

With the major works now completed, she sees the management team’s role as ensuring those renewed spaces are maintained to the same standard.

From hardware to service

The next phase of renewal could include upgrades to the tennis court, function room (The Astor Room) and barbecue area.

With most of the major physical works behind them, the council is shifting its attention from the property’s “hardware” to what Lodha calls its “software” — the services and experiences offered to residents.

An example is the 17 concierge staff at St Regis Residences, who are trained by Marriott, says Mohideen. They assist residents with many things — from carrying luggage or groceries to party planning and travel arrangements.

“These personal interactions and high levels of service are what set St Regis apart from other high-end condos,” says Mohideen.

The staff also provide umbrellas when it rains, and handle deliveries for residents.  “I travel a lot, and they will text me to let me know when I have a package, and ask me whether I would like it delivered to my apartment, or left for someone in my office to collect it,” says Lodha.

Rajoo says the concierge staff also help with decorations for birthday parties and Christmas gatherings, and even help clear up afterwards.

For Lodha, the greatest convenience is not having to carry his own luggage. “We all used to carry our own bags up to our apartments,” he says. “Now, when we arrive, we just leave them with the concierge because we’ve got used to having someone else carry our bags.”

Other smaller touches are also being considered, such as offering residents cold beverages and towels in the common areas. “The idea is to build that sense of appreciation where residents feel welcomed, wanted and special,” says Lodha.

The long game

For the owners, the AEI was ultimately about more than refreshing a development that had begun to show its age. It was also about deciding what kind of development St Regis Residences should be as it enters its next decade.

Protecting the long-term value of their homes was part of that equation from the outset. Marriott describes refurbishing its branded residences as a way to strengthen brand equity, improve the owner experience and protect owners’ investment.

“In several ways, the council went beyond Marriott’s brand standards to achieve the best outcome,” says Mohideen.

The council also feels St Regis Residences has not received the market recognition it deserves.

Only three transactions have taken place at St Regis Residences so far this year, based on caveats lodged. In March, a fifth-floor unit of 2,594 sq ft changed hands for $6.485 million ($2,500 psf), while a 2,153 sq ft unit on the ninth floor sold for $5.5 million ($2,555 psf). The latest transaction, in September, was for a 2,142 sq ft unit on the 16th floor that fetched $5.8 million ($2,708 psf).

“As a council, we are acutely conscious that [St Regis Residences] has not been given as much love as it should by the market, and therefore, that’s something that we are focused on rectifying,” says Lodha.

The approach has also made the council more conscious that maintaining an ageing luxury development cannot be a one-off exercise.

For now, the neighbouring construction at the redevelopment of Tanglin Shopping Centre may cause some inconvenience for nearby residents. But once it is complete, they will have access to new amenities, including “a massive performing arts theatre and art museum”, says Lodha. “So it is a short-term pain, and I would hope that it results in long-term gain.”

This perspective also underpins the AEI — accepting short-term disruption and continued investment to preserve the appeal and relevance of St Regis Residences over time.

title: Asia data centre boom vulnerable to US policies, Jardine says
article:
(Oct 9): Asia’s booming data-centre industry faces growing political risks as billions of dollars in investment hinge on a handful of US technology giants whose ability to operate globally could be upended by Washington’s increasingly unpredictable stance toward China, according to the chief of one of Hong Kong’s biggest conglomerates.

“The risk we think the most about at this point is actually political risk,” Jardine Matheson Holdings Ltd chief executive officer Lincoln Pan told the Milken Asia Summit in Singapore on Friday. “If you look at this debate about the US and China and the significant bets many people are making around this sector, particularly around data centres and AI large language models coming out of the US, it’s a highly concentrated bet on the stability of US data policy.”

Private equity giants including Blackstone Inc and KKR & Co have poured billions of dollars into Asian data centres, betting that the explosive growth of artificial intelligence and cloud computing will fuel demand for computing capacity for years to come.

While Asia’s digital infrastructure will struggle to keep pace with that demand, those facilities depend heavily on US hyperscalers that operate and are influenced significantly by US government policy, said Pan, whose company has real estate investments across Asia through its Hongkong Land unit.

Whether US-domiciled companies will be allowed to operate globally with the same degree of stability and certainty over the next decade is “a highly, highly uncertain risk that no one can underwrite,” he said.

President Donald Trump has been pushing AI investment in a race with China, even as some AI companies call for slower development and a public backlash over data centres emerges. China remains Asia’s biggest market for data centres, while outside the mainland, Western cloud providers account for about 70% of hyperscaler demand and Chinese players about 30%, according to a McKinsey report in June.

See also: Asia’s largest IT firm shrugs off latest US immigration curbs

Pan’s remarks come as Firmus Grid Ltd abandoned its attempt at one of Australia’s biggest-ever initial public offerings, after the Nvidia Corp-backed data centre company failed to lure global investors who have grown increasingly skittish over frothy AI valuations. Much of Firmus’ valuation was based on the company successfully building a pipeline of data centres across Asia serving customers such as Meta Platforms Inc and OpenAI.

The uncertainty extends beyond data centres to the broader AI investment boom. Despite the flood of capital into the sector, Jim Coulter, executive chairman of TPG Inc, cautioned that investors should resist assuming today’s winners and business models are already clear, saying the three most important words in AI are “I don’t know.”

See also: TCS profit beats estimates as IT deals start trickling in

Speaking on the same panel, Coulter likened investing in AI to the chaos of playing pinball, with more traditional investment akin to the repetition of 10-pin bowling.

“We have a number of themes that are very long-term themes that we’re still bowling,” he said. “But over the other side of the bowling alley, we’re playing pinball in AI because you have to shorten your cycle.”

title: Evergrande founder’s former ally sues to recoup US$1.3b
article:
(Oct 9): A former friend of China Evergrande Group founder Hui Ka Yan has entered a messy legal fight with the company’s liquidators over billions of Hong Kong dollars he says he lent to Hui over a decade.

Hong Kong property tycoon Cheung Chung Kiu on Thursday filed a lawsuit in Hong Kong’s high court demanding repayment of HK$10.1 billion (US$1.3 billion or $1.7 billion), citing verbal agreements Hui made between 2010 and 2020. The lawsuit comes days after Evergrande’s liquidators sued Cheung for about HK$18.7 billion based on transactions they found that appeared to capture funds Hui had transferred to Cheung between 2014 and 2020.

The two lawsuits offer fresh insight into the dealings of Hui’s network of billionaire friends that helped keep his business afloat. Cheung and Hui were known members of an elite poker group called the Big-Two Club and the two worked on several business deals together before Evergrande’s property empire collapsed and Hui was eventually sentenced to life in prison.

Evergrande’s liquidators are continuing to widen the net as they work to recoup cash for creditors, in this case turning to a former ally who may have received some of the company’s money. In 2024, they successfully froze the assets of Hui’s ex-wife and other former Evergrande executives.

In his suit, Cheung claims that he lent a total of HK$29 billion to Hui, of which about HK$18.7 billion was repaid in a series of transactions. Hui confirmed in writing that he still owed Cheung HK$10.1 billion as of Nov 15, 2022, according to the court filing.

Representatives for CC Land Holdings Ltd, where Cheung serves as chairman, and Evergrande’s liquidators didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

title: Chinese bonds become source of cheap money for global borrowers
article:
(Oct 9): China is letting a wave of cheap money flow across its borders, turning the country into a rare source of low-cost funding for foreign borrowers.

Regulators have approved the proceeds from more than 40% of panda bonds sold so far this year to be taken offshore, the highest share on record, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. That amounts to as much as 130 billion yuan (US$19 billion or $24.3 billion), also an all-time high. Panda bonds are yuan-denominated bonds issued in mainland China by overseas borrowers.

The shift echoes Japan decades ago, when rock-bottom yields and a glut of domestic savings sent capital pouring overseas — though China’s flows remain a tiny fraction of that. Subdued inflation and a weak economy have pushed rates lower as borrowing costs rise elsewhere, while Beijing is also loosening its grip on cross-border flows as it seeks a bigger global role for the yuan.

“Panda issuers are simply finding borrowing costs in the onshore renminbi market increasingly competitive versus those elsewhere,” said Dariusz Kowalczyk, head of cross-asset strategy for Asia at Banco Bilbao Vizcaya Argentaria SA. Beijing has also eased restrictions on taking the proceeds offshore as part of its push to boost the renminbi’s international use, he added.

The gap in borrowing costs is wide. China’s 10-year government bond yield stood at 1.68% on Friday, compared with 5.24% for US Treasuries and 3.02% for Japanese government bonds of the same maturity.

See also: China and Apec define regional trade

A few years ago, the panda bond market was dominated by the offshore entities of Chinese companies and foreign carmakers funding their China operations. Now the market has gone global, drawing Belt and Road partners including Hungary, Slovenia, Kazakhstan, Pakistan and Indonesia, as well as lenders such as Deutsche Bank AG, Morgan Stanley and Crédit Agricole SA.

Foreign issuers raised 115.5 billion yuan through Oct 8, twice as much as in all of last year, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. They now make up 47% of the market, up from 13% three years ago.

See also: China’s growth target has become a trap

More are on the way. Australia’s Fortescue Ltd. is weighing a three billion yuan debut, while Brazilian iron ore giant Vale SA is considering a similar move. UBS Group AG raised two billion yuan at just 1.78% in August, the lowest coupon on record for a five-year panda bond from a foreign financial institution.

Demand is growing offshore as well. Sales of dim sum bonds — yuan-denominated debt issued outside mainland China — have already surpassed last year’s record, reaching one trillion yuan, while non-Chinese issuers’ share has risen to 35% from 23%, data compiled by Bloomberg show.

It’s not just bonds. Chinese banks are also extending cheaper yuan credit across borders, competing more aggressively with global lenders. State-owned financial institutions from Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan are currently in talks to raise fresh yuan-denominated loans, according to people familiar with the matter, who asked not to be identified discussing private matters.

None of this happens without Beijing’s approval. Regulators announced rules in late 2022 allowing panda bond issuers to convert their proceeds into foreign currencies, whether for use in China or abroad.

Part of the motive is Beijing’s effort to internationalise the renminbi. A deeper yuan financing market gives foreign borrowers another source of funding while encouraging more trade, investment and financing in the Chinese currency, helping reduce China’s reliance on the dollar-based financial system.

Another reason is China’s persistent trade surplus. The country earns more from exports than it spends on imports, resulting in a large pool of domestic savings that needs somewhere to go. Panda bonds provide an outlet, allowing Chinese investors to lend to foreign companies and governments in yuan.

“Panda bonds are meant to recycle China’s current account surpluses,” said Timothy Tan, a Bloomberg Intelligence strategist. The market is still small, but Tan expects it to grow as China pushes for more trade to be settled in renminbi. That would boost demand for yuan reserves and leave companies with more of the currency to invest, he added.

A strong currency makes that easier to allow. The yuan’s more than 6% gain against the dollar over the past year has eased fears of capital flight that previously made regulators wary of letting money leave the country. But it also raises repayment costs for borrowers who swap yuan proceeds into foreign currencies. Hedging that risk costs about 3%, eroding much of the saving.

Borrowers using yuan for Chinese trade can avoid that cost. The currency settled 29% of China’s goods trade in the first half, up one percentage point from a year earlier.

“If you are genuinely raising yuan to settle yuan-denominated trade, you could save the hedging cost,” said Samuel Tse, senior economist at DBS Group Holdings Ltd. “You raise yuan, you use yuan, and suddenly that extra cost stays in your pocket.”

Japan offers a glimpse of where cheap currency funding can lead. Tokyo opened its financial markets and promoted wider use of the yen in the 1980s. Years of ultra-low interest rates later turned the yen into a major source of cheap global funding. China is taking a more controlled route, promoting wider yuan use while keeping restrictions on capital flows and managing the exchange rate.

With China’s borrowing costs well below those in the US, the appeal could persist. And as its trade ties deepen, more borrowers will have a natural use for the yuan.

“This could gradually strengthen China’s role from a major trading nation that mainly operates within a dollar-centred system into a provider of global funding, settlement and investment alternatives,” said Wei Li, head of multi-asset investments at BNP Paribas Securities (China).

title: DayOne in early talks with banks for potential US$500 mil bond — Bloomberg
article:
(Oct 9): DayOne Data Centers Ltd has been in preliminary talks for weeks with banks about a potential US$500 million ($640 billion) bond offering, according to people familiar with the matter, as the Singapore-based company ramps up fundraising amid growing demand for artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure.

The firm intends to push on with the discussions even after one of its project partners, Nvidia Corp-backed Firmus Grid Ltd, dropped an initial public offering plan in Australia this week, the people said, who asked not to be identified discussing private information.

Proceeds from the planned bond sale would be used for project financing, the people said. There were no details on which project or projects the money would be for. Citigroup Inc is the lead arranger for the deal and the data centre operator could go to the market as early as next year, the people said.

Representatives for DayOne and Citigroup declined to comment.

DayOne joins an increasing number of companies that are part of the broad AI buildout with plans to tap the debt market, banking on surging demand. But the failure of Firmus’ share sale attempt, in what would have been one of Australia’s largest IPOs, shows how global investors are starting to push back against what they see are frothy AI valuations.

The proceeds from Firmus’ listing would have funded purchases of graphics processing units for its first data centre project in Batam, Indonesia, that it’s developing with DayOne as part of an eight-year partnership with Nvidia.

See also: Treasury 10-year yield hits highest since 2002 on rate outlook

DayOne filed for a US IPO earlier this week and has been considering to raise around US$5 billion.

AI-related data centre spending could reach US$2.9 trillion between 2025 and 2028, with around half requiring external financing, which is driving debt issuance, according to Morgan Stanley.

If DayOne taps the bond market, it would be among the first data centre firms in Asia Pacific to do so and would help others in the business to draw on larger pools of capital beyond bank financing.

See also: Paramount said to draw US$109 bil of demand for high-grade bond deal

Ahead of its planned bond offering, DayOne has closed half of a US$7 billion-equivalent loan — one of the largest AI-linked borrowings in Asia — with more than 30 lenders participating. The upsized part of the loan, valued at US$3.7 billion-equivalent, was split into a RM5.5 billion ($1.73 billion) tranche and a US$2.4 billion portion.

DayOne has also been seeking a HK$1.86 billion (US$237 million or $300 million) loan for a Hong Kong data centre. In August, the company obtained a four-year $530 million to develop its first buildout in Singapore.

Other companies in the region have been aggressively raising money from the debt market to fund their AI ambitions. Billionaire Masayoshi Son’s SoftBank Group Corp last month raised the equivalent of US$11.1 billion in one of the largest corporate junk-bond offerings on record.

Once an international affiliate of Chinese data centre operator GDS Holdings Ltd, DayOne was previously known as GDS International before rebranding last year. It has brought in international investors, including SoftBank Vision Fund, Coatue Management and Ken Griffin and closed a US$4.5 billion Series C funding round in June.

Apart from Indonesia, the company is operating or developing data centres in Singapore, Malaysia, Japan, Hong Kong, Thailand and Finland, according to the company’s website.

title: Nobel Peace Prize bets for Navalny widow surge on Polymarket
article:
(Oct 9): Bets for who will take home the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize surged overnight on Polymarket, echoing similar events a year ago when a website hacking likely leaked the winner’s name.

Yulia Navalnaya, the widow of the late Russian opposition leader Alexey Navalny, has suddenly emerged as the frontrunner in betting on the Polymarket platform before the announcement due later on Friday.

Her odds went as high as 65.5% at one point, now sitting at around 46% with more than US$1.7 million in betting volume. The event overall has volume of just over

US$30 million.

Last year, a leak of Nobel Peace Prize laureate María Corina Machado’s name triggered an unusual betting surge on the Polymarket platform hours before she was unveiled as the award recipient. The Venezuelan opposition leader hadn’t previously been considered a favourite for the 2025 prize.

An investigation by the Norwegian Nobel Institute assisted by security authorities later concluded that an individual or a state actor may have illegally gained access to its website in a cyber breach.

Navalnaya, from exile, has carried on her husband’s campaign after his February 2024 death in an Arctic prison which his supporters and Western governments blamed on the authoritarian regime of Russian President Vladimir Putin.

See also: Germany and France push trade weapon to deny access to China

Arguably the most prestigious prize in global diplomacy, the Nobel Peace Prize has stirred more controversy. Last year, US President Donald Trump, who has long coveted the award, aggressively campaigned to obtain the award, in vain. Earlier this year, Machado gifted her medal to Trump, stunning Norway.

The Nobel prizes are annual awards for achievements in physics, chemistry, medicine, peace and literature. They were established in the will of Alfred Nobel, the Swedish inventor of dynamite who died in 1896.

All except the Peace Prize are awarded in Stockholm, and this year’s awards come with 12 million kronor of money.

title: Yuan hits four-year high versus basket as PBOC backs FX policy
article:
(Oct 9): The yuan advanced to a four-year high against a basket of its trading partners’ currencies after the People’s Bank of China (PBOC) rejected claims of undervaluation and defended its exchange-rate management.

The Bloomberg replica of the CFETS RMB Index rose to 103.9 on Friday, its highest level since April 2022, bringing its year-to-date gain to over 5%. The Chinese currency also sits near a multi-year peak versus the dollar and more than a one-year high against the euro.

The PBOC issued its clearest rebuttal yet against claims that the yuan is artificially undervalued, accusations that have intensified as China’s surging trade surplus draws fresh international scrutiny. The central bank noted that Chinese trade has become significantly less sensitive to currency swings, suggesting past rounds of appreciation did not disrupt trade performance. Still, the currency’s steady appreciation may help Beijing defuse some of that diplomatic tension.

“This may suggest that the PBOC will be comfortable with further yuan strength even as they disagree on the extent of the currency’s undervaluation,” said Khoon Goh, head of Asia research at Australia & New Zealand Banking Group.

The PBOC set the yuan’s reference rate at the strongest level since 2023 on Friday. The so-called fixing defines onshore yuan’s trading range by 2% around it.

See also: Dollar enjoys best month since June on Fed’s inflation fight

Goh expects the market to remain focused on daily fixings. “Pay attention to what they do, rather than what they say,” he said.

The central bank’s action followed a detailed policy document released on Thursday, in which the PBOC rejected using currency appreciation to address global imbalances and issued a rare rebuttal against undervaluation claims. The timing coincides with EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic’s two-day negotiations in Beijing with Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao, though the document made no direct mention of the talks.

Some strategists view the policy stance as a signal that Beijing favours managed strength over rapid adjustment.

See also: Yen strengthens past 157 per dollar, outperforming G-10 peers

“Our sense is that Beijing is still pursuing a gradual and measured path of yuan appreciation, rather than a one-off adjustment,” said Christopher Wong, strategist at Oversea-Chinese Banking Corp. “The authorities appear comfortable with a stronger currency but remain mindful of the pace of gain.”

title: Franklin Templeton sees short-term debt as sweet spot for AI
article:
(Oct 9): Franklin Templeton chief executive officer Jenny Johnson said short-term debt issued by major technology companies offers investment opportunities in artificial intelligence, citing strong cash flows and balance sheets.

Johnson said these companies are well funded not just with traditional creditors. The debt structure now includes off-balance-sheet instruments guaranteed by hyperscalers and suppliers who also act as lenders, making it “very complex.” Longer-term holdings also expose investors to advances in technology that may be uncertain.

“Going longer-term on those would be a little bit more scary for me,” she said in a Bloomberg TV interview from the sidelines of the Milken Institute Asia Summit in Singapore. “But you know, two-year paper at nine, pretty dang good!”

The AI story has yet to transform traditional business sectors, and the real productivity gains are still ahead, Johnson said. The current 2% productivity gains in the US reflect technologies that have been around for the last two decades, and it will take time for AI to work its way into the system.

“The AI story has not played out at all in sectors and traditional businesses,” Johnson said. “That is to come.”

Johnson pointed to healthcare as an example of early AI impact beginning to materialise, with companies reporting a bigger pipeline of potential drug discoveries and greater precision in clinical trials that could lead to higher efficacy and faster regulatory approval.

title: Indonesia cuts travel spending as energy costs pressure budget
article:
(Oct 9): Indonesia is tightening government spending towards year-end, ordering ministries and agencies to cut unspent travel allocations by 30% as higher oil prices and costly flagship programmes put pressure on the budget.

The budget deficit widened to 1.24% of gross domestic product (GDP) at the end of September, with Finance Minister Suahasil Nazara saying on Friday the government remains on track to meet its full-year outlook for a deficit of around 2.8% of GDP.

Higher oil prices, stronger domestic demand for subsidised fuel and liquified petrolueum gas, and a shift to monthly payments have pushed energy subsidy and compensation payments to 377 trillion rupiah as of end-September, up more than 50% from the same period last year.

Indonesia’s average realised crude price is expected to rise further from the current US$92 per barrel, already well above this year’s budget assumption of US$70, Suahasil said.

“And if it rises, then subsidies will also increase,” Suahasil said in a briefing. “All of this has a direct impact on the state budget, and we must certainly absorb these costs and ensure that payments are made.”

The spending curbs underscore the challenge facing the government as it funds programmes including free meals and village cooperatives while keeping the budget deficit below the legal ceiling of 3% of GDP.

See also: Why the US-China trade truce matters

The finance ministry said in a circular dated Oct 8 that the travel cuts apply to unspent allocations as of that date. Agencies must also defer spending on new vehicles, official housing and office renovations, prioritize virtual meetings and limit non-essential trips.

The measures aim to align government spending with development priorities while protecting public services and ensuring agencies meet planned targets, Sudarto, the ministry’s director general of state budget, said at the same briefing.

The government is also accelerating tax refunds for businesses that need cash flow, particularly labour-intensive industries and smaller firms, Suahasil said. The faster payouts are expected to moderate domestic value-added tax revenue as refunds are paid out more quickly.

See also: The OECD should be reclaimed, not abandoned

Separately, the government is seeking new sources of revenue. Indonesia plans to introduce a levy on sugar-sweetened drinks in the second half of 2027, targeting revenue of 1.7 trillion rupiah, Djaka Budi Utama, the director general of customs and excise, said at the briefing. The rate and technical details are still being discussed.

title: Asia’s largest IT firm shrugs off latest US immigration curbs
article:
(Oct 9): Asia’s largest provider of software outsourcing services shrugged off the Trump administration’s latest curbs on visa-based immigration, saying the fresh restrictions won’t affect its hiring or business strategy.

India’s Tata Consultancy Services Ltd said it will continue to step up local hiring in the US, including graduates. The firm reiterated it intends to hire 15,000 people in the US over the next five years, according to a statement on Friday.

The Trump administration on Thursday announced restrictions on the Permanent Labor Certification Program, or PERM, which allows companies to sponsor a foreigner who has been working in the US under the H-1B and other visa holders to become a legal permanent resident, the first step to becoming a US citizen. Officials singled out Microsoft Corp and several Indian IT firms including TCS as having abused the program.

“Our PERM applications were in single digits in the last two years and hence we do not expect the suspension of the program to impact our workforce strategy and customer engagements,” TCS said.

Shares of TCS climbed 4.2% in early Mumbai trading, while rivals Wipro Ltd and Infosys Ltd also advanced. Late Thursday, TCS reported quarterly profit that topped analysts’ estimates.

Silicon Valley’s reliance on foreign workers has long been a flashpoint in the debate over immigration. Since Donald Trump’s return to office last year, the administration has seized on those concerns and pressed tech giants to do more to train and hire US workers.

See also: TCS profit beats estimates as IT deals start trickling in

As part of that effort, Trump has moved to make it harder for companies to use H-1B visas to attract foreign talent, targeting a major source of workers for the industry. The changes have included proposals for US$100,000 filing fees for most candidates and tightening the rules of how the H-1B visas are awarded in an annual lottery, giving priority to companies offering the highest salaries.

The PERM suspensions announced on Thursday targeted Microsoft, Adobe Inc as well as Indian software services giants including TCS, Infosys, Wipro and HCL Technologies Ltd. Representatives of Infosys, Wipro and HCL didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

While the latest measures do not cancel the current H-1B visas, it would mean thousands of Indian engineers working in the US for the likes of TCS and Infosys would likely be forced to leave after the expiry of their work visas. Smaller US tech firms, unaffected by the new policy, could benefit though — by poaching Indian talent.

See also: Samsung profit up almost nine-fold with memory chip windfall

In the near term, IT service providers affected by the curbs may have to rely more heavily on local US talent and subcontracting, potentially increasing hiring and compliance costs, said Sumit Singhania, head of research at Bajaj Broking.

Longer term, more tech work could move outside of the US, potentially benefiting IT services providers’ profit margins, analysts at SBI Securities said in a note.

Indian outsourcers have traditionally used H-1B visas to move engineers and developers to service clients in the US, their largest market. But over the years, they’ve cut back their reliance on the visa program and hired more locally, Indian IT services lobby ground Nasscom said in a statement.

“Consequently, the number of employees transitioning from H-1B visas to permanent residency through the PERM process is also relatively limited,” it said.

title: Gold steadies as traders assess US-Iran tensions, Fed rate path
article:
(Oct 9): Gold was steady after rising moderately the previous day, as traders assessed Middle East tensions following President Donald Trump’s comments that the US wouldn’t attack Iran before November midterm elections. 

 

Bullion traded near US$4,145 an ounce, recovering from a two-month low seen earlier this week, after Trump said the US was having “productive discussions” with Iran, without offering details. Benchmark oil prices declined, though a hurricane menacing production in the Gulf of Mexico kept risks elevated.

Trump’s comments came even as Iran ramped up the pace of attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz this week, raising fresh concerns over a war now in its eighth month. That’s renewed inflation worries over rising energy costs, which has prompted some central banks to tighten monetary policy and weighed on the non-yielding precious metal.

Traders are expecting US borrowing costs to stay unchanged later this month but increase over the medium term. Federal Reserve Bank of St Louis President Alberto Musalem signalled on Thursday that interest rates should increase over the next six to nine months to help inflation return to the central bank’s 2% target, but stopped short of endorsing a move at this month’s policy meeting.

Gold was 0.3% higher at US$4,144.05 an ounce as of 8:00am Singapore time, while silver was 0.6% higher at US$59.54 an ounce, after falling 1% in the earlier session. Platinum and palladium edged higher. The Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index, a gauge of the US currency, was little changed.

title: Asian stocks set to fall on tech, oil edges lower
article:
(Oct 9) : Asian tech stocks are set to come under pressure, tracking a selloff in US chipmakers as speculation over OpenAI’s revenue revived concerns about the sustainability of the artificial-intelligence spending boom.

Equity-index futures pointed to losses in tech-heavy Japan and South Korea, while those for Australia signaled gains. US stock futures edged higher in early Asian trading after technology shares led Wall Street lower. The Nasdaq 100 sank 1.4%, its worst day in seven weeks, while a gauge of chipmakers slumped 3.4%.

The selloff followed a Financial Times report that OpenAI’s annualized revenue was US$20 billion below previously signaled levels. The ChatGPT maker is on track for roughly US$50 billion, according to people familiar with the matter, versus reports last month of nearly US$70 billion. Oracle Corp. also slid on a report it was trucking natural gas to server farms to ease power bottlenecks.

Elsewhere, Firmus Grid Ltd., an Australian data center company backed by Nvidia Corp., is set to postpone its initial public offering, and the company is weighing a private funding round instead, according to people familiar with the matter. The move is an ominous sign for other proposed data center listings, according to analysts.

The OpenAI revenue questions add to concerns over AI spending as elevated borrowing costs make the vast sums flowing into data centers and computing infrastructure harder to justify. Investors are increasingly looking for evidence that revenue can keep pace with the investment required to develop and run AI models.

“Investors are becoming a bit skeptical about how long this huge AI spending can last with borrowing costs rising in a significant way,” said Matt Maley at Miller Tabak.

See also: Oil declines after Trump says no Iran attacks before midterm

US oil edged lower after Brent surged on Thursday as fresh Iranian tanker attacks threatened to curtail a recent recovery in Middle East flows. The global benchmark jumped over 4% to settle above US$104 a barrel. The dollar was steady.

Treasuries advanced on Thursday after solid demand at a 30-year debt auction pulled long-dated yields back from more than two-decade highs. The rally extended after President Donald Trump said he would hold off on attacking Iran again until after the US midterm elections on Nov. 3.

The gains provided some respite from a months-long selloff in longer-term debt, fueled by concerns that the Iran war will keep energy prices and inflation elevated, alongside mounting worries over government finances.

See also: RBI signals further rate hikes as price pressures intensify

The outlook for rates remained under pressure, however, as Federal Reserve officials signaled more tightening ahead. Governor Christopher Waller said further increases will probably be needed to bring inflation under control, while St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said rates should rise over the next six to nine months without endorsing a move this month.

“To bring inflation back to target in a timely manner, more monetary policy firming will be required,” Musalem said Thursday at a Bloomberg event in New York.

Still, the weakness remained concentrated in technology rather than spreading across the broader market, highlighting the benefits of diversification. More than two-thirds of S&P 500 members advanced, while small-cap shares were little changed as investors rotated toward defensive sectors.

“My biggest surprise is the tech selloff remains concentrated, with more than two-thirds of S&P 500 constituents higher and small caps close to flat,” said Chris Murphy, co-head of derivatives strategy at Susquehanna International Group. “Strength in staples and low-volatility stocks points to rotation toward defensives rather than broad-based equity selling.”

title: Oil declines after Trump says no Iran attacks before midterm
article:
(Oct 9) : Oil fell after President Donald Trump said the US would not attack Iran ahead of November’s midterm elections.

West Texas Intermediate dropped toward US$91 barrel after climbing 3.6% on Thursday, while Brent closed above US$104. The US leader cited what he said were “productive discussions” with the Islamic Republic, while also saying that crude oil was flowing through the Strait of Hormuz in record volumes.

After Trump’s remarks, the New York Times reported that the US had drawn up plans for three days of strikes. The Pentagon had developed plans to hit drone and missile arsenals, energy facilities and other sites, the newspaper said.

Crude has had a volatile start to October as the US-Iran war drags on, with futures buffeted by rising flows from the Middle East, a pick-up in vessel attacks, and tightness in product markets. The fall-out from soaring freight rates, and renewed fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Tehran-backed Houthis in Yemen, have added further cross-currents to the market.

Beyond the Middle East, traders were also tracking Hurricane Isaias, which is gathering strength and expected to make landfall along the northern US Gulf Coast late Friday or early Saturday, with Alabama, Mississippi and the Florida Panhandle at risk. Producers in the US Gulf of Mexico have shut in about 1.3 million barrels a day of crude production, more than 60% of output in the region.
